Looking at a network is often the quickest way to understand it: a drawing shows at a glance
whether a graph falls apart into groups, has a few dominant hubs, or is a long chain. EdgeCase draws
graphs with `plot()`, which computes a layout and renders the graph as a self-contained SVG image.
The image needs no JavaScript to display, so it works the same in a Jupyter notebook, a Quarto
document, a web page, or a file on disk.

This page covers the mechanics of `plot()`: what it returns, how to save a drawing, and how to
control its size, labels, edges, and theme. The pages that follow go further:
[Layouts](layouts.qmd) describes the algorithms that place the nodes,
[Aesthetics](aesthetics.qmd) maps colors and sizes to data, and
[Interactive widgets](interactive.qmd) covers the zoomable, draggable alternatives.

## A first plot

With no arguments, `plot()` places the nodes with a force-directed layout and draws every node and
edge. The karate club makes a good first example. `label_by="label"` shows the node labels, the
member numbers `"0"` to `"33"`, instead of the internal node IDs, and `seed=` fixes the random
starting positions of the layout so that the picture is the same every time:

```{python}
import edgecase as ec
import polars as pl

karate = ec.karate_club()
karate.plot(label_by="label", seed=1)
```

The layout treats the edges as springs that pull linked nodes together and the nodes as charges
that push each other apart, so closely knit groups end up near each other. The two halves of the
club are already visible: the instructor, `"0"`, sits among one group on the right, and the
administrator, `"33"`, among the other on the left. Before the drawing is rendered, nodes that would
overlap are pushed apart, and straight edges that would pass through a node are bent around it,
unless so many edges need it that the bends would crowd the drawing.

The image is not entirely static: in a notebook or a web page, hovering over a node or an edge shows
a tooltip with its attributes, which makes it easy to identify a node of interest without labelling
every one. Above 2,000 nodes or edges, the output is made lean: an edge shows its tooltip only when
the pointer is right on it, with no wider margin around it to catch the pointer, and nodes and edges
of the same color and width share that styling rather than each carrying a copy. This keeps a graph
of ten thousand edges to a megabyte or two.

## Displaying and saving plots

`plot()` returns a `StepPlayer` object, the same kind of object that the traversal and step
replays return (see [Traversals](traversals.qmd) and [The step log](step-log.qmd)). Notebooks
and Quarto documents display it automatically when it is the last expression of a cell. Elsewhere,
its `svg` property holds the raw SVG markup as a string:

```{python}
player = karate.plot(seed=1)
player, player.svg[:60]
```

There are two ways to save a drawing to a file. The `output=` argument saves it as part of the call,
and the `save()` method saves an existing plot. In both cases, the extension picks the format. A
path ending in `.html` writes a small web page that keeps the hover tooltips, `.svg` writes the plain
SVG, which can be opened by vector graphics editors and placed in documents and slides, and `.png`
writes an image at twice the plot's size, sharp on high-density screens:

```{python}
#| eval: false
karate.plot(label_by="label", seed=1, output="karate.svg")

player = karate.plot(label_by="label", seed=1)
player.save("karate.html")
player.save("karate.png")
```

The plot is returned either way, so `output=` can be used in a notebook cell that also displays the
plot. A large graph's plot can show its edges and nodes as images, or in the viewer (see
[Larger graphs](#larger-graphs)); its `.svg` file then holds them as SVG elements all the same.

## Canvas and node size

The canvas is 700 by 500 pixels by default, and `width=` and `height=` change it. The force and
random layouts spread the nodes over the whole canvas, so a wide canvas gives a wide drawing, and
the force layout is turned so that a long graph lies along the canvas's longer side. Positions from
a layout method keep their proportions (see [Layouts](layouts.qmd)).

The node radius is chosen automatically from the canvas area and the number of nodes, from 16 pixels
on small graphs down to 3.5 pixels on large ones, and edge widths likewise shrink as the graph grows.
The defaults, `node_size=16` and `edge_width=1.2`, stand for "automatic"; any other value is used as
given. Smaller nodes leave more room for the edges, which helps on graphs where the structure of the
links matters more than the individual nodes. The 62 bottlenose dolphins of Doubtful Sound, drawn
with small nodes and no labels:

```{python}
dolphins = ec.dolphins()
dolphins.plot(show_labels=False, node_size=7, seed=1)
```

The drawing shows the two communities of the dolphin population, linked by only a few animals.
`edge_opacity=`, 0.4 by default, controls how transparent the edges are. Translucent edges keep
dense regions readable, since areas where many edges cross appear darker rather than solid.

## Node labels

The text drawn on each node is chosen by `label_by=`:

- `"id"` shows the node IDs, which is the default
- `"label"` shows the node labels, or the ID of nodes without a label
- the name of a node attribute shows its value, or the ID of nodes without the attribute
- `"degree"` shows the number of edges of each node

A graph of up to 50 nodes has every label drawn. A larger one has 30 of them, those of the
highlighted nodes first, then of the larger nodes and of the nodes with the most edges, leaving out
any label that would cover one drawn before it. `max_labels=` sets how many are drawn at most, so
that `max_labels=0` draws none and a large number draws as many as fit. The 77 characters of *Les
Misérables*, with the names of the best connected:

```{python}
ec.les_miserables().plot(label_by="label", seed=2)
```

`show_labels=False` turns the text off altogether. A name that no node has is an error rather than
being silently ignored, so a misspelled attribute is caught immediately:

```{python}
try:
    karate.plot(label_by="faktion")
except ValueError as error:
    print(error)
```

Passing `label_by=` on every call gets repetitive when a graph should always be shown with its
labels. [`set_node_attr_to_display()`](../reference/Graph.set_node_attr_to_display.qmd) records a
preference on the graph itself, which `plot()` then uses whenever `label_by=` isn't given:

```{python}
florentine = ec.florentine_families()
florentine.set_node_attr_to_display("label")
florentine.plot(seed=1)
```

The marriage network of the Florentine families of the fifteenth century shows the Medici at its
center, linked to families that are mostly not linked to each other: a position that let the Medici
broker between the other families, as discussed in [Centrality](centrality.qmd). The display
preference is stored with the graph, so it applies to every later plot until it is changed, and
`set_node_attr_to_display()` without an argument clears it.

## Directed graphs and multigraphs

A directed graph is drawn with an arrowhead at the target end of each edge. Graphs with parallel
edges, reciprocal edges, and self-loops need some care, since a straight line can show only one edge
between two nodes; `plot()` fans parallel and reciprocal edges out as separate curves, and draws a
self-loop as a small loop above its node. A small supply network has all three:

```{python}
supply = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_edges(
    [
        ("Farm", "Mill"),
        ("Farm", "Mill"),
        ("Mill", "Bakery"),
        ("Mill", "Cafe"),
        ("Bakery", "Cafe"),
        ("Cafe", "Bakery"),
        ("Cafe", "Cafe"),
    ],
    auto_create_nodes=True,
)
supply.plot(label_by="label", seed=1, width=500, height=350)
```

The two deliveries from the farm to the mill appear as two curves side by side, the bakery's
deliveries to the café and the café's orders to the bakery as two curves in opposite directions, and
the café's own coffee roasting as a loop. Only the edges are drawn differently; the layout itself
ignores edge directions and multiplicities.

## Edge labels

`edge_label_by=` names an edge attribute to write along each edge, which is useful when the edges
are of several kinds or carry a value worth reading. Edges without the attribute are left
unlabelled. In a small organization, some edges record who manages whom and others who mentors whom:

```{python}
org = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_edges(
    [
        ("Dana", "Eli"),
        ("Dana", "Fay"),
        ("Eli", "Gus"),
        ("Eli", "Hal"),
        ("Fay", "Ivy"),
        ("Gus", "Hal"),
        ("Fay", "Eli"),
    ],
    auto_create_nodes=True,
)
org.set_edge_attrs("rel", "manages", edge_ids=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
org.set_edge_attrs("rel", "mentors", edge_ids=[6, 7])
org.plot(label_by="label", edge_label_by="rel", seed=1, width=500, height=350)
```

Edge labels are drawn small, at the middle of each edge, so they work best on small graphs whose
edges are reasonably long. The edge weight is not an edge attribute in this sense, since it is
stored separately from the other attributes (see [The graph model](graph-model.qmd)); to show
weights or other numbers, copy them to an attribute first, as the road network examples of
[Paths and distances](paths.qmd) do with their distances.

## Choosing a layout

The `layout=` argument chooses how the nodes are placed:

- `"force"`, the default, is a force-directed layout that places linked nodes near each other
- `"circular"` places the nodes evenly around a circle
- `"random"` scatters the nodes uniformly over the canvas
- any other string names a node attribute that holds `(x, y)` coordinates

The circular layout shows every edge as a chord of the circle, so dense and sparse patterns are
easy to compare, and the positions don't depend on a random seed:

```{python}
florentine.plot(layout="circular")
```

The nodes go around the circle in the order a depth-first search meets them, so linked nodes
tend to sit close together and many edges run along the rim, which makes the drawing easier to
read; [Layouts](layouts.qmd#circles-and-shells) shows how to arrange the circle in another order.
The fourth option is the most flexible. The `layout_*()` methods, such as
[`layout_kamada_kawai()`](../reference/Graph.layout_kamada_kawai.qmd) or
[`layout_bipartite()`](../reference/Graph.layout_bipartite.qmd), compute positions with more
specialized algorithms and store them in the `"pos"` node attribute, which `layout="pos"` then
draws. Positions that come with the data, such as geographic coordinates, can be stored and drawn
the same way. [Layouts](layouts.qmd) describes all of them.

### Reproducible drawings

The force and random layouts start from random positions, so two calls give different pictures
unless `seed=` is passed. The same seed on the same graph always gives the same picture, which is
what a document or a report needs: the text can then refer to the left or the right of the drawing.
Different seeds give drawings that are rotated, reflected, or arranged differently, and it is
worth trying a few seeds when a drawing will be published, since some arrangements show the
structure more clearly than others.

## Curved edges

`curved_edges=True` draws every edge as a gentle curve rather than a straight line. Curves make it
easier to follow individual edges where many of them meet at a node, and give a softer look:

```{python}
florentine.plot(curved_edges=True, seed=1)
```

With curved edges, the edges are no longer routed around the nodes, and parallel edges between the
same two nodes are drawn along the same curve, so straight edges are the better choice for
multigraphs.

## Overlaps and edge routing

Two adjustments are made after the layout and before drawing, and both can be turned off or tuned.

`node_overlap=` controls overlapping nodes. The default, `"remove"`, pushes nodes apart until they
are at least 2 pixels from each other, and a number sets a different minimum gap. `"allow"` keeps
the positions exactly as the layout computed them. The adjustment applies to the force and random
layouts, and not to positions given by a `"pos"` attribute, which are taken to be meaningful.

`edge_routing=` controls edges that pass through nodes. The default, `"auto"`, bends such an edge
so that it clears the nodes in its way by 3 pixels, as long as the bends in the whole drawing stay
few, and draws direct lines otherwise. `"around"` always bends them, and a number always bends them
with that clearance. `"straight"` draws every edge as a direct line. Turning both adjustments off shows the raw layout of the dolphin
network:

```{python}
dolphins.plot(show_labels=False, node_size=7, node_overlap="allow", edge_routing="straight", seed=1)
```

The positions are the same as in the earlier dolphin plot, but the nodes in the dense center now
overlap, and some edges run underneath nodes that they don't belong to. The raw layout is faster to
compute, and it is the faithful choice when the distances between nodes are meant to be read,
since overlap removal moves nodes slightly.

## Themes

`theme="dark"` draws the graph on a dark background with light labels and tooltips, to suit
dark-mode notebooks and presentation slides. The co-appearance network of the characters of *Les
Misérables*:

```{python}
miserables = ec.les_miserables()
miserables.plot(theme="dark", show_labels=False, seed=2)
```

The bishop Myriel and the minor characters of his story form the fan on the left, linked to the
rest of the novel only through Myriel himself. Valjean is the hub at the center, and the dense
cluster to the lower right holds Marius and the students of the ABC society. The theme changes only the background, the default node and edge colors, and
the text; the palettes for colored nodes are described in [Aesthetics](aesthetics.qmd).

`shade=True` shades the nodes as spheres, lit from the upper left: each is lighter there and darker
toward the far side, with its own color in between. It looks the same in the SVG, the images and
the viewer:

```{python}
ec.karate_club().plot(color_by="faction", shade=True, seed=1)
```

## Larger graphs

`plot()` draws graphs of tens of thousands of nodes and edges in a few seconds, into a few
megabytes: the 4,941 nodes of the power grid network take about a second. The drawing is another
matter, as beyond a few hundred nodes and a few thousand edges it becomes a dense ball in which
little can be seen. For the 198 bands and 2,742 links of the jazz network, small nodes, no labels,
and faint edges are already needed:

```{python}
jazz = ec.jazz()
jazz.plot(show_labels=False, node_size=4, edge_opacity=0.15, edge_routing="straight", seed=1)
```

A dense core of musicians who played with many others is surrounded by a sparser periphery. Edge
routing is turned off here: in a dense graph almost every edge passes some node, and the detours
make the drawing busier and the SVG several times larger without making it clearer. In still more
crowded drawings, `"auto"` routing leaves the edges straight by itself.

A graph whose SVG would pass 10 MB or 20,000 elements, more than a notebook or a web page should
hold, is drawn differently: its edges and nodes become images, which stay within a few megabytes
however large the graph is, and show where many edges cross by how dark they get. The labels and the
legend stay text, but the nodes and edges have no tooltips. The wiki-vote network, with 103,689
edges, is drawn this way:

```{python}
ec.wiki_vote().plot(show_labels=False, seed=1)
```

At this size, the drawing shows the graph's overall shape rather than its nodes: a dense core, a
fringe of users with few votes whose edges fan in toward it, and, below and to the right, the 23
pairs and triples of users whose votes link them to no one else. `backend="png"` draws any graph
this way, and `backend="svg"` keeps the SVG elements, however many there are, up to 200 MB, past
which a plot raises an error rather than being drawn. An output that passes 10 MB even as images,
with thousands of labels, comes with a warning.

How the edges show where they cross is `edge_tone=`. With `"over"`, each edge is drawn over the
ones under it, as SVG strokes stack up, so that where many cross the drawing goes solid. With
`"log"`, the images show the edges' density on a log scale, from a lone edge's opacity up to opaque
at the densest point, so that a dense core still shows how dense each part of it is. The default,
`"auto"`, is `"log"` for images and `"over"` for SVG, which can't draw the log tone; given
`edge_tone="log"`, `backend="auto"` draws images whatever the graph's size, and `backend="svg"`
raises an error.

`backend="viewer"` draws the edges and nodes in the browser instead, with WebGL, so that the drawing
can be panned and zoomed. Drag it to pan, and zoom with the buttons in its corner, the `+`, `-` and
`0` keys, a double click (with Shift to zoom out), or the mouse wheel once the plot has been clicked;
until then the wheel scrolls the page. As in the images, the edges show their density, in the tone
that `backend="auto"` would draw them in unless `edge_tone=` says otherwise, with the log tone
opaque at the densest point in view, and the nodes can be as small as a pixel. Zooming in on the core of the wiki-vote network pulls apart edges
that the whole view runs together:

```{python}
ec.wiki_vote().plot(show_labels=False, seed=1, backend="viewer")
```

The last button in the corner, or the `F` key, shows the plot full screen, where the wheel zooms
without a click; `Esc` or `F` again leaves it. Where a page doesn't allow full screen, as in some
notebooks, the plot fills the window instead.

The button below it, Settings, opens a panel of controls in the terms of `plot()`'s arguments: the
node size and shading under Nodes, the edges' opacity, width and curve (and, under More, their
tone) under Edges, whether the labels are
shown and how many under Labels, and the theme (and, under More, the legend) under View. A changed control is marked, with a button that resets it. In a wide
plot, or full screen, the panel docks at the side; in a smaller one it slides over the graph, and a
click outside it or `Esc` closes it. "Copy as code" copies the `plot()` call that draws what the
viewer shows, with the changed arguments, to paste back into the notebook. The plot is framed for
its first settings, so a call with much larger nodes can frame the graph a little differently.

A column of text, such as this page's, is narrow for a large graph. With the viewer, `width=` can
also be a CSS length, such as `"100%"`, for a plot as wide as its container, at the height of
`height=`. In a Quarto document, a cell option such as `#| column: page` widens the container
beyond the text column:

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| column: page
ec.wiki_vote().plot(show_labels=False, seed=1, backend="viewer", width="100%", height=600)
```

The layout then keeps the default canvas's shape at that height, and the viewer fits it to the
box. The legend keeps its size, at the top right, and where the plot is too small for it, it folds
into a button that shows it.

Hovering over a node or an edge outlines it and shows its tooltip, the same as in the SVG; on a
touch screen, tap it. Dragging hides the tooltip until the drag ends.

Clicking a node or an edge selects it, and the viewer draws the selection as `highlight=` and
`highlight_edges=` would: the selected nodes, and the ends of the selected edges, in the accent
color (or their own, with `color_by=`), and the rest muted. Shift and a click adds a node or an
edge to the selection, or takes it out; a loop drawn with Shift held, or with the lasso button
below the zoom buttons, adds the nodes inside it. `Esc`, or a click on nothing, clears the
selection and brings back the plot's own highlighting. "Copy as code" writes the selection as those
two arguments, so the selection can be pasted back:

```{python}
#| eval: false
ec.karate_club().plot(highlight={1, 34}, highlight_edges=[(1, 2)], seed=1, backend="viewer")
```

The search, the small pill beside the zoom buttons (or the `/` key), finds a node by its ID or its
label as it is typed; choosing one, with the arrow keys and Enter or with a click, flies to the
node and selects it.

The legend is a control too: clicking a swatch hides its nodes, or its edges, along with the edges
of the hidden nodes, and clicking it again shows them. Alt (Option) and a click shows the swatch's
group alone, and again shows them all. The filters belong to the view, not to `plot()`, so "Copy as
code" leaves them out and the panel says so.

The labels stay the same size as the view zooms, and the viewer chooses them again, by the same
rule as the SVG, for the part of the graph in view: zooming in on a crowded region shows the
labels that had no room in the whole view. An edge's label is written along it, where it is long
enough on screen.

The viewer draws arrowheads and self-loops as the SVG does, but doesn't route edges around nodes.
The legend is drawn over it as SVG. The HTML holds the viewer's
code, the drawing's data, the labels and the tooltips, compressed, about 2.7 MB for the wiki-vote
network, and
the viewer stays quick with hundreds of thousands of edges, in any browser with WebGL 2. The plot's `svg`
property and `.svg` file hold the SVG elements, and its `.png` file is an image as for the other
backends.

For graphs the size of the jazz network and larger, several strategies help:

- draw a meaningful part of the graph, such as a k-core, an ego network, or one community, with
  the methods of [Transforming graphs](transforming.qmd)
- collapse groups of nodes into single nodes with `quotient_graph()`, so that the drawing shows how
  the groups are linked
- color the nodes by community or size them by centrality, so that the structure stands out even
  when individual nodes can't be told apart (see [Aesthetics](aesthetics.qmd))
- use `plot_cosmo()`, which lays out and draws graphs of hundreds of thousands of nodes on the GPU
  in the browser (see [Interactive widgets](interactive.qmd))

## Summary

| Argument | Controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `layout=` | node placement: `"force"`, `"circular"`, `"random"`, or a position attribute | `"force"` |
| `seed=` | the random start of the force and random layouts | `None` |
| `width=`, `height=` | canvas size in pixels, or for the viewer a CSS width such as `"100%"` | `700`, `500` |
| `node_size=`, `edge_width=` | node radius and edge width, automatic at their defaults | `16`, `1.2` |
| `edge_opacity=` | edge transparency, from 0 to 1 | `0.4` |
| `label_by=`, `show_labels=` | the node text | `None`, `True` |
| `max_labels=` | the most node labels drawn, all up to 50 nodes and 30 past that at `None` | `None` |
| `edge_label_by=` | an edge attribute to write along the edges | `None` |
| `curved_edges=` | curved rather than straight edges | `False` |
| `node_overlap=`, `edge_routing=` | overlap removal and routing around nodes | `"remove"`, `"auto"` |
| `theme=` | `"auto"`, `"light"` or `"dark"` | `None` (automatic on screen, light in files) |
| `shade=` | nodes shaded as spheres rather than flat | `False` |
| `edge_tone=` | how crossing edges show: `"over"`, or `"log"` for images and the viewer | `"auto"` |
| `backend=` | SVG elements (`"svg"`), images (`"png"`) or the viewer (`"viewer"`) for the edges and nodes | `"auto"` |
| `output=` | a path to save to, as `.svg`, `.html` or `.png` | `None` |

The arguments for colors and sizes, `color_by=`, `size_by=`, `edge_color_by=`, `palette=`, and
`cross_community_color=`, are covered in [Aesthetics](aesthetics.qmd).
